attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, not a quote of anyone else.

semantics.note: The proposition matches the clause. It sits in a rhetorical list, but the clause itself is a firm claim about what AI can do now.

contract.note: Reading the claim as AI reliably taking over only a small share of ordinary work is a fair, ordinary reading. The May 2025 period and the lack of any numeric threshold are the evaluator's choices, so the interpretation decides the result.

evidence.note: ILO exposure index, May 2025. It says full job automation is limited, but it models potential exposure rather than measuring work actually automated.
Danish users saved about 2.8% of work hours in late 2023–2024. That is an earlier period, a narrow set of occupations, and realized time savings rather than capability.

Anthropic is describing its own data: 43% of sampled conversation tasks were automation-style. The sample is conversations, not work time, and the company says it can't verify work use or later editing.

reviews.rationale: No item measures how much ordinary work was reliably automated in May 2025. The ILO figures are modeled exposure, the Danish savings are older and narrower, and Anthropic's 43% is a company's own conversation data with stated limits. The evidence leans toward limited automation but doesn't settle the claim under the contract's measure.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Verbatim restatement. It combines a conceptual point about what the job is, a hedged 'might' that isn't scored, and a firm claim that there is no proof yet. Only that last claim and the conceptual point can be checked.

contract.note: The evaluator sets the bar for 'proof' and decides whether reduced hiring or freelance demand counts as 'taking jobs'. The reading is ordinary, but the result depends on it.

evidence.note: Salesforce's CEO on its Feb 2025 earnings call: no new engineer hires this year, crediting coding tools. This is the company talking about itself, with no entry-level breakdown and no independent check that AI replaced workers.
Danish study finding near-zero effects on earnings and hours through 2024. It can't show there was no displacement of junior engineers elsewhere.
Freelance coding postings fell about 20% (published 2024). That is freelance demand, not entry-level engineering jobs, and it doesn't address outsourcing.

reviews.rationale: None of the items credibly ties entry-level engineering job losses to AI while ruling out other causes. The packet also can't show that no such proof existed by June 2025. The conceptual point that coding isn't the whole job isn't directly tested.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Correctly isolates the firm 'yet to be proof' clause and leaves out the hedged 'might affect' part.

contract.note: Requiring credible causal evidence specific to entry-level work is a fair reading of 'proof'. Whether avoided hiring or freelance work counts is the evaluator's choice.

evidence.note: Salesforce's CFO, reported May 2025, said AI means fewer engineer hires. This is the company describing itself, with no entry-level breakdown and no ruling-out of other causes.
SignalFire: new-grad tech hiring has fallen sharply. It cites budgets and AI together and doesn't isolate an AI effect.
Freelance study: novice postings fell in a broad skill group that includes programming. It measures freelance postings, not entry-level software engineering jobs.

reviews.rationale: Each candidate counterexample falls short: a company statement without verification, descriptive data that blames several causes, and a freelance study that isn't specific to software engineering. That leans toward the claim, but the packet admits it can't show there was no qualifying proof by June 16, 2025.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Verbatim. 'Can cause' is read as a claim that a legal-risk mechanism exists now, not as a hedged forecast.

contract.note: The ordinary reading asks only for some speed gain, usable rough output and a credible route to legal harm, which is fair to the speaker.

evidence.note: Peer-reviewed study: Whisper transcription was slightly faster than humans (8.5 vs 8.8 hours) with high quality. The speed gain is modest.
GPT-4 translation study, fieldwork March–June 2024, published before the evaluation date: editing machine output averaged 14% faster. Gains varied by person and heavy editing was needed.
Whisper hallucination study: invented speech could expose employers to disability-discrimination liability in hiring. That is a concrete legal-risk mechanism.

reviews.rationale: Before the post, generative systems gave some speed gains in transcription (slight) and translation (14% on average) with usable output, and there was a documented mechanism for legal risk from hallucinated transcripts. The gains are modest and uneven, but the claim requires no particular size.
